searchText: I suspect there are two reasons: 1. It makes the chain useable more quickly by getting the newest stuff (most likely to be needed) first. 2. If you have a trusted block that you are starting your sync from, you can walk the header chain backwards as newer blocks point at older blocks but older blocks don't point at newer blocks. After asking Gakonst the answer is actually that otherwise you could perform a long-range attack with leaked pks from past validations to build a false canonical chain quote > So we should document this a bit better, but in PoS, you take the last header and you go backwards. If you start from an old header, you cannot know if it is a block that’s been produced due to a long-range attack, until you get to the recent blocks. PoW clients also walked backwards I believe. But yes, that falls into (2). Under PoS you *must* start from a recent trusted block (more recent than week subjectivity range). That quote isn't *quite* right. You don't need the *latest* header, you just need "something more recent than the weak subjectivity threshold". Which means "somewhat recent" (days to weeks old).

I suspect there are two reasons:
1. It makes the chain useable more quickly by getting the newest stuff (most likely to be needed) first.
2. If you have a trusted block that you are starting your sync from, you can walk the header chain backwards as newer blocks point at older blocks but older blocks don't point at newer blocks.
